title: Singleness
hook: Paul and Jesus were single; celibacy is honored as a calling

segments.voice: Yesterday, marriage: a sacrament for some churches, a covenant for others, faithful love for all of them. Your line was two becoming one. Which couple did you hold in mind, and did you reach out? Day one thousand two hundred seventeen.

A wedding reception, table nine. The single friend gets the question again, from an aunt, kindly meant: so when's it your turn? Everyone laughs. The friend laughs too, a half second late. Here's something that might surprise that aunt. The Gospels never mention a wife for Jesus. And Paul tells the Corinthians he wishes more people could live as he does: unmarried. Two figures at the heart of the Christian story, and neither one is shown at a wedding of his own. Today: singleness.

Start with Paul's own words to the Corinthians, in the King James Bible: "For I would that all men were even as I myself. But every man hath his proper gift of God, one after this manner, and another after that." Notice the word gift. Paul isn't saying single people are waiting for real life to begin, and he isn't saying married people have settled for less. Each way of life is a gift, and each person has their own. He even gives a practical reason: the unmarried person can give undivided attention to the things of the Lord. Jesus speaks of some who give up marriage for the kingdom of heaven's sake, and adds, he that is able to receive it, let him receive it. Not everyone, then. But some, as a calling. Christians have honored that calling in different ways. Catholic and Orthodox monks and nuns make vows of celibacy. In the Latin Catholic church, priests are ordinarily celibate; Orthodox priests may marry before they are ordained, though their bishops are chosen from the celibate. Protestant churches don't require celibacy of their ministers, and they too honor single believers who serve with their whole lives. And there's an older promise still, from Isaiah, to those who would never have children: "Even unto them will I give in mine house and within my walls a place and a name better than of sons and of daughters." A place and a name. Not someday, after a wedding. Already. A single life, in this reading, isn't half of something.

Here's the practice: honor a single friend. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone in your life who is single: by choice, by circumstance, after loss, or simply not yet. Set aside every question about their dating life. Instead, look at what their life already holds. Their work. The people they show up for. The things they do that nobody else in your circle does. Name one of those to yourself, clearly. If you are the single one, you can turn this toward yourself. If you pray, you can give thanks for them. The bell holds the time.
Singleness. In Paul's words, a gift from God like marriage is a gift, and for some, a calling to serve with an undivided heart.
Your line: whole already. Today, tell a single friend the one thing you named, and ask them nothing about dating. Day one thousand two hundred seventeen.
